---
title: "1.1 What is a fluid?"
---

{{< include ../_checkpoint-widget.qmd >}}

## The big idea

A solid, pushed sideways, deforms a bit and pushes back. A fluid **cannot**
push back against shear — it deforms *continuously*, forever, under any
shear stress however small. What a fluid *can* do is set the **rate** of
that deformation, and the property that sets it is viscosity:

$$\tau = \mu \frac{du}{dy}.$$

## Think first

**Recall**

1. From solid mechanics: what does shear stress do to a block of steel, and what happens when you remove it?
2. Units check: what are the SI units of stress? Of a velocity gradient $du/dy$?

**Look ahead**

1. What single experiment separates "fluid" from "solid"?
2. Honey and water both flow. What, precisely, is different about them?
3. Why does the fluid touching a moving wall move *with* the wall?

## The defining experiment

Put a material between two plates and slide the top plate sideways. A
solid deforms to some angle and stops — internal stresses have risen to
balance your push, and if you let go, it (elastically) springs back. Do
the same to water and it never stops deforming: layer slides over layer
for as long as you keep pushing. That's the definition. **A fluid deforms
continuously under applied shear stress.** (This is why "fluid" covers
both liquids and gases — they differ in how they respond to *squeezing*,
not to shearing.)

So a fluid can't resist shear. What it *can* do is regulate how fast the
shearing proceeds. Slide the top plate at speed $U$ with a gap $h$, and
two experimental facts emerge. First, the fluid **sticks to both walls** —
zero velocity at the bottom plate, exactly $U$ at the top. This is the
*no-slip condition*, and it is not obvious; it took the 19th century a
long argument to accept it. (The molecular picture: fluid molecules
exchange momentum with the wall so thoroughly that the layer touching it
has no independent velocity of its own.) Second, for common fluids the
force needed is proportional to $U$ and inversely proportional to $h$ —
i.e., proportional to the velocity *gradient*:

$$\tau = \frac{F}{A} = \mu \frac{U}{h} = \mu \frac{du}{dy}.$$

The constant $\mu$ is the (dynamic) viscosity, units Pa·s, and it is the
fluid's entire personality in shear. Water: about $10^{-3}$ Pa·s. Honey:
about 5 — five *thousand* times more resistant to shearing, at nearly the
same density. Air: $1.8\times10^{-5}$, which is not zero, and Unit 7 is
largely about the outsized consequences of that not-zero.

::: {.column-margin}
Fluids obeying $\tau = \mu\, du/dy$ with constant $\mu$ are *Newtonian* —
water, air, oils, honey. Ketchup, blood, and paint are not (their
apparent $\mu$ changes with shear rate), which is a topic for a later
course and an excellent party fact.
:::

## Play with it

The plate experiment. The profile is a straight line (you'll prove *why*
in Unit 6 — for now it's an experimental fact) — and it's the **same**
line no matter what fluid fills the gap. What changes from fluid to fluid
is the force it takes to keep the plate moving:

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
fl_h_11 = 0.005   // 5 mm gap
fl_U_11 = 0.5     // 0.5 m/s plate speed
fl_A_11 = 0.1     // 0.1 m^2 plate area
fl_profile_11 = d3.range(51).map(i => ({
  y: fl_h_11 * i / 50 * 1000,      // mm
  u: fl_U_11 * i / 50 * 100        // cm/s
}))
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Plot.plot({
  width: 560, height: 260,
  x: {label: "u (cm/s)"},
  y: {label: "y (mm)"},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(fl_profile_11, {x: "u", y: "y", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.ruleY([0], {stroke: "black", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.ruleY([fl_h_11 * 1000], {stroke: "black", strokeWidth: 3}),
    Plot.text(["moving plate →"], {x: [20], y: [fl_h_11 * 1000 + 1.5]}),
    Plot.text(["fixed plate"], {x: [20], y: [-1.5]})
  ]
})
```

```{ojs}
//| echo: false
Inputs.table([
  {fluid: "Water", "μ (Pa·s)": 1e-3},
  {fluid: "SAE-30 oil", "μ (Pa·s)": 0.29},
  {fluid: "Honey", "μ (Pa·s)": 5}
].map(f => ({...f, "force to keep plate moving (N)": +(f["μ (Pa·s)"] * fl_U_11 / fl_h_11 * fl_A_11).toFixed(3)})))
```

Same profile, three very different forces. Keep that distinction; it will
matter every time you look at a velocity field and are tempted to think
you can see forces in it.

::: {.callout-important}
## The misconception to leave behind
"Viscous" does not mean "dense," and it does not mean "thick" in the
colloquial sense. Mercury is 13.6× denser than water and *less* viscous
than SAE-30 oil. Viscosity is about how hard neighboring layers grip each
other, not how much the fluid weighs. The two properties will play
opposite roles all semester (one drives inertia, one resists shear), and
their *ratio* is coming for you in module 2.1.
:::

## Earn it — 2 quick gates

Two predictions turn the definition into a number. An SAE-30-ish oil (μ = 0.29 Pa·s) fills a 1.0 mm gap under a 0.5 m × 0.5 m plate sliding at a steady 2.0 m/s. Ungraded; hints after a miss; **Show me** after two. Arguing about a gate with a classmate is the assignment, not a violation.

```{=html}
<div class="fl-reveal-all"></div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="Shear stress in the oil film?"
     data-answer="580" data-tol="0.03" data-units="Pa"
     data-hint="τ = μU/h — and h is one millimeter, not one meter. If you got 0.58, the gap bit you."
     data-solution="τ = 0.29 × 2.0 / 0.001 = 580 Pa, uniform across the film (linear profile)."
     data-target="wif-s2"></div>
```

::: {#wif-s2 .fl-hidden}
Same number at every height in the gap — the linear profile means one slope, one stress. Now buy the force.

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="Force needed to keep the plate moving?"
     data-answer="145" data-tol="0.03" data-units="N"
     data-hint="Force = stress × plate area. The 0.25 m² finally enters here — and only here."
     data-solution="F = τA = 580 × 0.25 = 145 N — about the weight of a small child, to slide one plate on one millimeter of oil."></div>
```

That pair — τ = μ(du/dy), then F = τA — is the whole Newtonian contract, and every viscosity problem in this course is one of these two lines wearing a costume.

:::

## Check yourself

<details><summary>**Q1.** You double the gap $h$ at the same plate speed. What happens to the force?</summary>
Halves: $\tau = \mu U/h$. The same total velocity difference spread over
more fluid is a gentler gradient — less shear everywhere.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q2.** Cold maple syrup barely pours; warm it and it flows freely. Did its density change much?</summary>
Barely (a percent or so). Viscosity, though, drops steeply with
temperature for liquids — often several-fold over a kitchen temperature
range. Density and viscosity are independent dials.
</details>

<details><summary>**Q3.** If a fluid "can't resist shear," why does stirring cold honey take real effort?</summary>
It resists the *rate*, not the deformation. Honey never wins — it always
yields — but it charges a high price per unit speed. Stir slower and the
torque drops; a solid wouldn't offer that deal.
</details>

## Bring to class

One sentence: what experiment would you run to decide whether mystery
substance X (silly putty? mayonnaise? glass?) is a fluid — and what result
settles it?
